The treatise states that *kaukṛtya* (remorse) has the nature of regret, ranging from the sense of having done wrong to subsequent remorse.
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, the detailed explanation, which is divided into two parts.
First is the explanation of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*).
Next, vitarka and vicāra are explained;
each of these consists of two types,
the first of which is their distinction.
The subsequent summary and the detailed exposition constitute two parts. "Remorse" refers to what is called "bad action," for its essence is itself the cause.
Thus, various treatises state that *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is not *vipratisāra* (regret); rather,
the essential nature of *vipratisāra* is that which consists of retrospective regret.
This may be understood from the text. As for the essential nature of *kaukṛtya* (remorse), what constitutes its essence?
"Kau" means regret;
it is the feeling of aversion toward an action that has been performed.
When one feels aversion toward the various actions one has performed and subsequently regrets them,
that is the nature of remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
If the action performed was evil, it is termed "evil conduct" (*akukṛta*).
Thus, the essence of regret (*kaukṛtya*) is exclusively wholesome,
because it consists solely in the remorse for having committed an evil act.
If one feels aversion toward what one has done, how could its essence not be regret?
It is said that this [remorse] is the cause of regret (*kaukṛtya*).
If regret arises only after an evil deed has already been committed,
what then is the essential nature of that evil deed which is not itself regret?
This point should be reflected upon. Herein, there is an interpretation:
this [state] is merely aversion (*nirveda*).
If that were so, then aversion would necessarily pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
Why is it exclusively wholesome?
This school does not hold such a view;
the masters of the *Abhidharma-samaya-prakaraṇa-śāstra* maintain that the nature of aversion is exclusively wholesome.

If it were identical to that [mind], there would be the same obstacles as mentioned before. Some say that this "aversion" (nirveda) is the mind of investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-citta*), and that mental factors have no separate ontological nature.
In the Mahāyāna, aversion is said to pervade all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
This does not contradict the meaning. If that is so, upon what are the foundations for the renunciation (*nirveda*) associated with the wholesome, the defiled, and the indeterminate established?
The sixth fascicle previously stated that within the wholesome, renunciation is a portion of non-attachment (*alobha*).
According to that [view], the essence of defiled revulsion is precisely hatred (*dveṣa*),
because one only comes to loathe wholesome states by way of hating and being resentful toward them.
The delight in superior unwholesome states is craving (*rāga*).

Disgust for inferior and evil phenomena is also a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*). If that is so, how is disgust that is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*) established? It is simply a neutral desire (*chanda*);
although it does not give rise to a longing for action, it is still a form of desire.
Because one also gives rise to desire regarding that which is not performed, it is called "disgust" (*nirveda*).
Just as with faith (*śraddhā*) and lack of faith (*aśraddhā*), there are only wholesome and afflicted states, but no indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) ones.
Indeterminate faith is simply desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*).
This case should also be understood in the same way.
The causes of regret are precisely the two preceding factors of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*) and desire (*chanda*).
Nevertheless, it is taught that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) can be of all three moral natures.
Speaking from the perspective of its result,
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) pertains to all three moral natures. Alternatively, some explain that "that which was done" (*kṛta*) constitutes the object.
To feel aversion toward what has been done is the meaning of "regretting evil.
Here, "what is done" refers to the action that gives rise to such regret for evil.
This is precisely the cause of regret.
"Cause" refers to the object;
for it is by depending on the causal act and depending upon that [object] that regret arises.
Because the term "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) is used to refer generally to its object, it is said that remorse in general is the cause of regret;
in reality, however, "remorse" (*ku*) is itself regret (*kṛtya*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "remorse" (*akuśala*) is shame (*hrī*).
Because it resists evil,
the unwholesome is shamelessness (*āhrīkya*);
for it disregards what is noble and good.
The indeterminate [state] is wisdom (*prajñā*),
because it is subsumed under the wisdom of deportment and the wisdom of craftsmanship. Furthermore, it is explained that all three natures have wisdom as their essence,
because they perform the function of discerning and deliberating.
Regarding the statement that one first fails to act and only later feels regret:
this refers to the sequence of cause and effect across preceding and succeeding moments; alternatively, it is spoken of as "before" and "after" even when they occur simultaneously.
Nevertheless, it is by virtue of an object that the mind arises.
According to the treatise, its function is to obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*).
The commentary states:
This is not the characteristic of cessation (*śamatha*) among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*),
because the characteristic of cessation is common to both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because it causes the mind to settle.
What is now called "stopping" (śamatha) refers to *śamatha* itself;
it is that which can cause the mind to abide, not that which causes it to settle down.

Mental misconduct (*kaukṛtya*) is the cause;
the essence of regret (*kaukṛtya*) is the fruit.
Regret is termed "mental misconduct."
It is named after its cause.
First, the evil deeds committed reveal the cause;
subsequently, the resulting remorse clarifies the fruit.
As previously explained in the treatise:
"Regretting what was not done in the past... this is my remorse."
The commentary states:
This now demonstrates that even when one perceives what does not exist, remorse arises.
Regarding the phrase "that which was done":
It is not necessary that remorse must concern something previously done; that which is named *kaukṛtya* (evil-doing/remorse) also includes regretting what was not previously done.
For example, one might express regret by saying, "I previously did not perform such a task; this is my *kaukṛtya*."
Such matters as these were committed by me through my own misconduct.
"Committing" means placing;
it was through my own misconduct that I placed myself in this situation.
The worldly convention states that "regret" (*kaukṛtya*) and "remorse" (*vippaṭisāra*) are synonymous terms for the same entity.
This is explained in detail in the eleventh chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that its essential nature consists of longing for what has been done and for what has not been done.
The statement that "obstructive karma also obstructs śamatha" is exactly the same as this.

"Sleep" (middha) refers to that which has the nature of reaching a state of dullness and contraction.
The commentary states:
"By means of this single term, the various teachings [are encompassed]."
This causes the body to lack self-mastery;
for one falls asleep even while sitting,
and so forth, such that one does not even perceive being shaken by another.
This has the nature of making the mind extremely obscure, light, and superficial;
it is because it is neither clear nor sharp, but rather dull and heavy. Thus says the treatise.
Its function is to obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The commentary states:
this refers to *vipaśyanā* itself.
This is a specific hindrance to meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*);
it is not like the hindrances among the *nīvaraṇas* which can obstruct *pragraha*.
*Pragraha* applies to both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), causing the mind to become uplifted.
The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Teachings) agrees with this. The treatise states:
"This is because, in the state of sleep, [the mind] functions through a single gateway."
The commentary states:
This explains the aforementioned lack of mastery. "Lack of mastery over the body" means one cannot exercise independent control;
"lack of mastery over the mind" means the mind is extremely dull and inferior, functioning through only a single gateway.
In the single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are no five sensory consciousnesses;
because it functions in a state of darkness and inferiority, there is no time when it is clear and distinct.
To distinguish it from other minds, there are also the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because there are times when it is obscured, inferior, and dull, lacking clarity. The treatise states:
"Dull" excludes that which exists in meditative concentration; it does not mean that its essence and function are non-existent.
The commentary states:
Although it involves focused attention on the subtle,
it is nonetheless distinct from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is because it is characterized solely by dullness (*mūḍha*). Therefore, "dullness" serves to distinguish it from the state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Although other distracted states of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) possess darkness, they are not so designated.
Nor is it slight or casual,
for it is also profound and grave; thus,
it is briefly distinguished from the time of waking.
Because it is extensive at the time of waking;
the eleventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states that its nature is "obscure and concise.
Nevertheless, in common parlance, people say, "You are sleeping."
Because it is also said that one is "asleep" during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*).

Alternatively, there is another interpretation: fearing that the Sautrāntika masters might establish [the term] as a mere designation (*prajñapti*) upon a collection of both general and specific [factors], the word "letting" (*pra-*) was placed [at the beginning].
The treatise states: Because it is said to possess a substantial entity (*dravya*), it can then perform functions such as causing the body and other faculties to lack autonomy;
this demonstrates that sleep is not without a substantial entity or function.
Because there is a state of non-consciousness that reaches association with the mind.
The commentary states:
In both worldly convention and the sacred teachings, even a state of non-consciousness is termed "sleep."
This is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
It is as stated in the treatise: "sleeping without consciousness.
This refers to that very state.
Because it is induced by sleep and resembles the state of being asleep even when one has awakened, it is also called "sleep.
How do we know that sleep exists as a distinct entity and is not simply a state of mindlessness?
Because it is like other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Since other hindrances are necessarily mental factors (*caitta*),
they are not entities lacking substantial reality (*avastuka*).
Regarding the five hindrances:
first, the hindrance of sensual desire;
second, the hindrance of ill will.
3. The hindrance of sloth and torpor;
4. The hindrance of restlessness and remorse;
5. The hindrance of doubt.
The meaning of "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) is that it obscures the mind, preventing the arising of virtue.
Through attachment to sense objects, it obstructs the delight in renunciation;
through aversion toward those who point out one's transgressions, it obstructs the awakening to right practice.
Torpor and drowsiness obstruct calm abiding by inducing mental sinking;
restlessness and remorse obstruct uplifting by inducing distraction;
and doubt, through its lack of certainty, obstructs the state of equanimity.
These five hindrances collectively obstruct three stages:
first, the aspiration for renunciation;
second, the cultivation of correct practice.
Subsequently, upon entering right concentration,
the cultivation of tranquility (śamatha), exertion (pragraha), and equanimity (upekṣā) are respectively hindered.
If one says that they are also called "hindrances" because they are caused by the hindrances, [that is so].
It is not necessarily a mental factor (*caitta*),
for it should be like the other *paryavasthānas*,
which are exclusively mental factors. There are eight types of *paryavasthānas*.
Lethargy, drowsiness, restlessness, remorse, envy, avarice, lack of shame, and lack of dread—
these repeatedly increase and entangle his mind.
Because they act as obstacles to the cultivation of the class of wholesome qualities:
the first two obstruct calm abiding (śamatha),
and the latter two obstruct exertion (pragraha).
Envy and avarice obstruct relinquishment;
for, within the sphere of stinginess and jealousy regarding one's own and others' welfare, they cause the mind to fluctuate repeatedly.
The equanimity that serves as an obstacle within the middle [dhyāna] is different from this;
it is designated "equanimity" because it refers to a state of mental balance that is neither suppressing nor uplifting.
Doubt is able to obstruct this.
This is called equanimity (*upekṣā*) because it is based on the equality of the two benefits;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) obstruct the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
One who possesses these two [qualities] lacks a sense of shame regarding the transgression of the various training rules (śikṣāpada). Therefore,
this hindrance (nīvaraṇa) and fetter (paryavasthāna) neither increase nor decrease.

There is an interpretation that these two [ignorance and craving] are branches of delusion (*moha*).
The commentary states:
The following provides a general explanation of the two [points].
There are four explanations in total;
this is the statement of the first master.
There is no separate entity; its very nature is delusion (*moha*). How is this known?
Because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter fifty-five, and other sources state that it is a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) and a derivative of delusion.
The same applies to the Abhidharma.
Regarding the statement that it "pervades the three natures":
because its substance consists of as many minds and mental factors as are present in those aggregates, it pervades the three natures.
Regarding the statement that "delusion exists only within the defiled," the *Śāstra* presents one interpretation which holds that this is not so,
as it is subsumed under both [the general category] and the specific portion of delusion.
The commentary states:
Because it also pertains to the wholesome;
if it were merely delusion (*moha*), [it would not be so].
How so? Since the wholesome consists of the aggregate total of mind and mental factors as its essence, one should state that these two defiled states have delusion (*moha*) as their essence;
for the wholesome is precisely the absence of delusion (*amoha*).
Because they are established as opposites [to the primary afflictions],
the fifty-five [mental factors] and so forth are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) from the perspective of their defiled aspect.
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharma* that [remorse] "encompasses the wholesome and so forth" because it is subsumed under the category of delusion (*moha*),
this indicates that it is not necessarily a part of delusion;
this is as explained in the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* concerning remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
It is said that [regret] has as its essence the longing for good or unwholesome deeds, whether defiled or undefiled;
it is not said to be indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Because that is a general statement,
the wholesome and the defiled take delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) as their respective essences.
Furthermore, within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because it is a collective enumeration, it is described as "general indeterminate."

It should be stated that [the mind] proceeds from regret (kaukṛtya) until the completion of the action.
Commentary says:
The two dharmas of regret (kaukṛtya) and volition (cetanā) constitute its essence.
Why are wisdom (prajñā) and volition its nature?
Because it clearly knows what has been done, it takes wisdom as its essence.
Because it deliberates upon what is to be done, volition (cetanā) constitutes its essence;
it does not consist of anything else, as the capacity of other factors is inferior.
Thus says the Treatise.

The commentary states:
Sleep has the two dharmas of thought (vitarka) and reflection (vicāra) as its essence.
Why is this so? Because one contemplates various dream-like objects;
for this reason, there is also that which is established based on other higher [states].
How is it known that these two have distinct bases?
Because these two phenomena do not possess separate substantial entities.

Because it is as previously stated,
and secondly, because of the scriptural teaching,

The treatises both state that it is "reaching" (*prāpti*) and state that it is a part of delusion (*moha*).
The commentary says:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Fifty-Fifth Chapter) states that because these two are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*),
their nature is merely nominal (*prajñapti-svabhāva*). Their defiled aspect resembles delusion (*moha*) and is its outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Just as with lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) and so forth, although their essential natures (*svabhāva*) exist separately, they are still said to be "parts of another" (*parabhāga*).
This accords with the statement in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya* that because it is a part of delusion (*moha*), it is conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*).
Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that a dream has desire (*chanda*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) as its two constituent factors.
That which was described as "predominant" is here described as "pervasive," because not all dream-minds possess desire.

As a gāthā says: "Because the characteristic and the characterized do not exist.
[The commentary] states:
This is the verse from the tenth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
From the perspective of reasoning, the mind (citta), mentation (manas),
and consciousness (vijñāna) can be said to be distinct, because they possess different characteristics according to their respective functions within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Because it is the ultimate truth in terms of the ultimate meaning,
its characteristics are not distinct.
The fourth ultimate meaning transcends words and conceptual thought.
Now, while the existence of distinction is negated, only the absence of distinction is asserted.
Since it is said to be beyond words, what difference could there be between distinction and non-distinction?
This is because the self-nature and characteristics of consciousness do not exist.
Because the defining characteristic does not exist, that which is defined also does not exist.
Both the defining characteristic and the characterized nature are established based upon consciousness;
when sought, they cannot be found.
Within consciousness, what constitutes the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and what the characterized (lakṣya)?
It is said that function is the characteristic and substance is the characterized.
If this function exists within the phenomena of conventional truth,
yet in the truly ultimate principle it is inexpressible by both mind and speech;
if one were to hold that there is a distinction based on the initial conventional [perspective], [it would be a mistake].
Regarding the four truths, there is no distinction in their underlying principle:
the first truth is such because its phenomena are like illusions;
the second truth is such because it possesses the nature of cause and effect.
Because the third gate of truth is devoid of self,
and the fourth gate of truth transcends both mind and speech,
neither possesses distinct characteristics.
Because, within the four truths, the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) lacks such things as substantial utility that could serve as defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa),
and thus lacks the entities (lakṣya) that would possess them;
whereas, in the second [truth], the conventional reality of the eight consciousnesses possesses distinctness.
The same applies to the three truths:
because the dependent nature, which is the characteristic of activity,
and the dependent dharma-substance, which is the characterized object, are both non-existent.
Alternatively, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is taken as the characteristic (lakṣaṇa),
and the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) as the characterized (lakṣya);
the seven consciousnesses are taken as the characteristics.
The eighth [consciousness] as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is likewise;
all should be considered in this way.
This is because the third conventional [consciousness] and the other seven can be distinguished as cause and effect through their mutual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The same applies to the two types of ultimate truth;
likewise, the fourth conventional truth corresponds to the fourth ultimate truth.
When analyzed through the gateway of the ultimate, the principle remains without distinction.
The gate of reality merely negates distinctions; it does not posit non-distinction.
Even this non-distinction is itself without distinction, for there is no non-distinction that is not [itself] distinct.
All of this should be contemplated.
Since there is no characterized object (*lakṣya*), how can there be a characterizing mark (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Since the characterizing mark does not exist, the characterized object likewise does not exist.
Therefore, there is no distinction between the eight consciousnesses as being either determinate or indeterminate.
